rule: Is the payment an EFT from a consumer account (Reg E coverage)?
payment_rail: Debit card, ATM, ACH, P2P apps, online bank transfers, prepaid
legal_trigger: Money left a checking, savings, prepaid or other consumer asset account that was opened mainly for personal, family or household use, by electronic means
obligation: If yes, run the Reg E rules (R-E series). If the money moved by check, wire, a securities trade, an automatic bank-initiated move between the customer's own accounts, or a one-off phone call to the bank with no recurring plan, Reg E does not cover it; route to the matching rail rules.
exceptions: Check-originated transfers (1005.3(c)(1)); Fedwire or similar wires (c)(3); securities and commodities transfers (c)(4); automatic intra-institution transfers (c)(5); phone-initiated transfers outside a written plan (c)(6); preauthorized transfers at institutions with $100M or less in assets (c)(7)
human_review_trigger: Business account; wire; brokerage; caller cannot say how money left; transfer mixes a wire with an online banking instruction
uncertainty: Online consumer wires: People v. Citibank (S.D.N.Y. 2025) held the consumer-to-bank leg can be an EFT; on appeal (see G-04).

rule: Who holds Reg E duties when a P2P app is involved
source_pinpoint: CFPB EFT FAQs, Coverage: Financial Institutions Q1-Q4; Unauthorized EFTs Q3, Q10, Q11; 12 CFR 1005.2(i)
legal_trigger: Transfer went through a P2P service linked to or holding a consumer account
obligation: The account-holding bank keeps full error-resolution duties even when a non-bank P2P provider initiated the transfer; a non-bank P2P provider that holds an account or issues an access device is also a financial institution. Draft the notice to the account-holding institution and, where applicable, to the P2P provider.
exceptions: Narrow service-provider rules where no agreement exists between institutions (FAQ Coverage FI Q1, Q4)
human_review_trigger: Bank and app each tell the caller to go to the other (CFPB found this practice unfair in the Block order, S24)
uncertainty: FAQs are a non-binding compliance aid (S19).

rule: Unauthorized EFT: initiated by someone other than the consumer, without actual authority, no benefit to consumer
source_pinpoint: 12 CFR 1005.2(m); 15 U.S.C. 1693a; Supp. I comments 2(m)-1 to 2(m)-5
legal_trigger: A person other than the account holder entered and sent the transfer, and the account holder got nothing from it
obligation: Treat as a candidate unauthorized EFT. Liability limits (R-E05 to R-E08) and error resolution (R-E09 to R-E13) apply.
exceptions: (1) Person the consumer furnished the access device to, until the consumer tells the institution that person is no longer authorized (comment 2(m)-2); (2) fraudulent intent by the consumer or anyone acting in concert; (3) transfers by the institution or its employee (comment 2(m)-1 says consumer is not liable for employee fraud)
human_review_trigger: Caller says a family member, caregiver or coworker made the payments; caller received any money from the transfer; any hint the caller shared in proceeds
uncertainty: Low on the text. Applying 'furnished' vs 'obtained by fraud' to real facts is contested (G-02, G-06).

rule: Access device or credentials obtained from the consumer by fraud or robbery: transfers by the fraudster are unauthorized
source_pinpoint: Supp. I comment 2(m)-3; comment 2(m)-4 (forced ATM use); CFPB EFT FAQs, Unauthorized EFTs Q4-Q6
payment_rail: All Reg E rails, incl. P2P credit-push
legal_trigger: Caller gave a code, password, PIN or card details to someone posing as a trusted party (bank, app support, utility), or credentials were stolen (breach, stolen phone), and that person then initiated the transfer
obligation: Treat as unauthorized: fraudulently induced sharing is not 'furnishing' the access device (FAQ Q6). Same treatment for credentials captured by watching through remote access or phishing (FAQ Q5).
exceptions: Consumer personally initiated the transfer (see R-E03); consumer acted in concert with the fraudster
human_review_trigger: Institution denied on the ground that the customer 'shared credentials' or 'authorized the device'; account agreement says anyone given access is deemed authorized (e.g., Chime I.D.3, S43)
uncertainty: Comment 2(m)-3 is an official interpretation; the FAQ applying it to codes is a compliance aid (S19) and the CFPB withdrew other guidance in 2025 (S20). FDIC examiners treated such denials as Reg E violations (S33, secondary). Green v. Capital One allowed such a claim at the pleading stage (S31, secondary).

rule: Consumer-initiated payment induced by a scam is not an unauthorized EFT under the current text
source_pinpoint: 12 CFR 1005.2(m) ('initiated by a person other than the consumer'); Wilkins v. Navy Federal (D.N.J. 2023)
payment_rail: P2P, online transfers, debit card, ACH credit-push
legal_trigger: The account holder entered and sent the payment themselves after being deceived about who the recipient was or what the payment was for
obligation: No federal reimbursement right on this basis. Screen other routes: (a) Zelle 'qualifying imposter scam' policy if Zelle and impostor of a bank, business or agency (R-P01); (b) card payments: Reg Z or network dispute (R-Z01 to R-Z05); (c) wrong amount or recipient caused by the system may be an 'incorrect EFT' (R-E04); (d) voluntary bank goodwill; (e) state-law and attorney review.
exceptions: If the scammer, not the consumer, pressed send (including via remote-access control), go to R-E02
deadline: None statutory for this route; still file promptly for any network or voluntary policy
human_review_trigger: Large loss; older or vulnerable caller; New York resident (state AG litigation, S28-S29); remote-access session where it is unclear who pressed send
uncertainty: High. Advocates and the NY AG press for liability; proposed federal bill (S47) died in 2024; no rule change. See G-01.

rule: Incorrect EFT and other non-fraud errors (wrong amount, wrong recipient through system or directory fault)
source_pinpoint: 12 CFR 1005.11(a)(1)(ii)-(vii); CFPB Supervisory Highlights Fall 2021 (token errors)
payment_rail: All Reg E rails, esp. P2P
legal_trigger: Payment went to someone other than the intended recipient because the P2P directory or institution data was wrong, or the amount differs from what the customer instructed
obligation: Treat as a notice of error; same timelines as R-E09 to R-E13. Investigation must look at whether funds reached the intended recipient, not just whether instructions were followed (S34, secondary).
exceptions: Sources reviewed do not address a consumer who typed the wrong handle when the directory data was correct; treat as uncertain
clock_start: Transmittal of first statement showing the error
human_review_trigger: Institution says it 'followed instructions' without checking delivery
uncertainty: Medium; the token-error position comes from a supervisory publication (S34, secondary).

rule: Liability conditions: no consumer liability unless access device accepted, identification method provided and disclosures given
legal_trigger: Institution seeks to hold the consumer liable for any part of an unauthorized EFT
obligation: If the institution has not met the 1005.6(a) conditions, consumer liability is zero. The institution carries the burden of proof (R-E15).
exceptions: None stated
human_review_trigger: Institution imposes any liability without showing disclosures were given
uncertainty: Low.

rule: $50 cap when lost or stolen access device is reported within 2 business days of learning of it
payment_rail: All Reg E rails with an access device (card, code, phone wallet)
legal_trigger: Card, PIN, code or device was lost or stolen and the consumer gave notice within 2 business days after learning of it
obligation: Consumer liability capped at the lesser of $50 or the unauthorized amount before notice.
exceptions: Lower liability under state law or agreement applies (1005.6(b)(6)); many card networks and banks offer $0 'zero liability' by contract (bank practice, not law)
clock_start: Day after the consumer learns of the loss or theft (the day learned is excluded; comment 6(b)(1)-3)
extension_rules: Extenuating circumstances such as extended travel or hospitalization (R-E08)
human_review_trigger: Institution counts the 2 days from the transaction date instead of the date the consumer learned of the loss
uncertainty: Low. 'Learning of the loss' is a fact question; a statement is a factor but not conclusive (comment 6(b)(1)-2).

rule: Up to $500 when the 2-business-day notice is missed; unlimited for later transfers after the 60-day statement window
source_pinpoint: 12 CFR 1005.6(b)(2), (b)(3); comments 6(b)(2)-1, 6(b)(3)-1, 6(b)(3)-2; Widjaja v. JPMorgan Chase (9th Cir. 2021)
legal_trigger: Notice came after 2 business days (tier 2) or after 60 days from transmittal of the statement showing the first unauthorized transfer (tier 3)
obligation: Tier 2: $50 for the first 2 business days plus later transfers the institution proves notice would have stopped, total capped at $500. Tier 3: consumer may be liable for transfers after the 60-day window and before notice, only if the institution shows they would not have occurred with timely notice. Transfers with no access device involved fall only under tier 3 (comment 6(b)(3)-2).
exceptions: Extension for extenuating circumstances (R-E08); lower state-law or contract liability; tiers can apply together (comment 6(b)-1)
deadline: Tier 2: after 2 business days. Tier 3: 60 days
clock_start: Tier 3: institution's transmittal of the periodic statement first showing an unauthorized transfer
human_review_trigger: Institution denies the whole claim (including transfers inside the 60 days) because notice came late
uncertainty: Low on text; Widjaja confirms the institution's causation burden for post-60-day losses.

rule: Negligence does not increase liability; agreements cannot impose more; extensions for extenuating circumstances; notice by any reasonable means
source_pinpoint: Comment 6(b)-2, 6(b)-3; 12 CFR 1005.6(b)(4), (b)(5); comments 6(b)(4)-1, 6(b)(5)-1 to -3; 15 U.S.C. 1693l (anti-waiver); CFPB FAQ Unauthorized EFTs Q7, Q8
legal_trigger: Institution cites customer carelessness (PIN written down, code shared) or contract terms to raise liability; or caller was hospitalized or traveling; or someone else reported for the caller
obligation: Liability depends only on timing of notice, not care. Time limits must be extended to a reasonable period for extenuating circumstances. Notice counts when the consumer takes reasonable steps, in person, by phone or in writing, even to a different address or number, and may be given by someone acting for the consumer.
exceptions: Institution may require documentation that a third party acts for the consumer (comment 6(b)(5)-2)
extension_rules: 'Reasonable period'; examples: extended travel or hospitalization
human_review_trigger: Denial letter cites negligence, 'gross negligence', or a contract clause; People v. Citibank kept alive a claim that a user agreement waived EFTA burden of proof (S26)
uncertainty: Low for negligence; the length of a 'reasonable' extension is fact-specific.

rule: Timely notice of error: received within 60 days after the statement first showing it
legal_trigger: Consumer gave oral or written notice identifying name and account and why they believe there is an error (type, date, amount where possible)
obligation: Institution must follow 1005.11 procedures. Account number not required if the institution can identify the account (comment 11(b)(1)-1). Institution may require notice at its disclosed number or address if it refers callers who use other channels (comment 11(b)(1)-6).
exceptions: Late notice: institution need not follow 1005.11, but for unauthorized EFTs it must still apply 1005.6 liability limits before imposing liability (comment 11(b)(1)-7). Prepaid accounts may use the alternative timing in R-E14.
clock_start: Institution's transmittal of the periodic statement first reflecting the error (held statements: date first made available, comment 11(b)(1)-3)
extension_rules: Error window itself has no extension clause; liability extension in R-E08 still applies
human_review_trigger: Institution rejected a claim as late without applying 1005.6
uncertainty: Low.

rule: Written confirmation may be required within 10 business days; investigation cannot wait for it or for a police report
source_pinpoint: 12 CFR 1005.11(b)(2), (c)(2)(i)(A); comments 11(b)(1)-2, 11(c)-2; CFPB FAQ Error Resolution Q4; FAQ Unauthorized EFTs Q9
legal_trigger: Consumer gave oral notice
obligation: Institution may require written confirmation within 10 business days if it told the consumer of the requirement and the address when the oral notice was given. It may request a signed statement but may not delay starting or finishing the investigation while waiting, and may not require a police report or a merchant contact before investigating.
exceptions: If written confirmation was required and not received in 10 business days, provisional credit is not required (1005.11(c)(2)(i)(A)); investigation must still proceed
extension_rules: Wrong-address confirmation must still be processed (comment 11(b)(2)-1)
human_review_trigger: Institution refused to start until it got an affidavit, notarized form or police report; told caller to contact the merchant or app first
uncertainty: Low for 'cannot delay'; whether an institution may later rely on a missing affidavit is untested in this guidance (see G-07).

rule: Investigation timelines and provisional credit
legal_trigger: Timely notice of error received
obligation: Determine within 10 business days, report within 3 business days after finishing, correct within 1 business day of finding an error. Or take up to 45 days if the account is provisionally credited within 10 business days (may withhold up to $50 for suspected unauthorized EFT if 1005.6(a) met), consumer told amount and date within 2 business days, with full use of funds.
exceptions: 20 business days instead of 10 when the transfer was within 30 days after the account's first deposit; 90 days instead of 45 for that case, for point-of-sale debit card transactions (not ATM), and for transfers not initiated within a state. No provisional credit if required written confirmation not received, or Regulation T account.
calendar_vs_business_days: 10/20 and 2/3/1 are business days; 45/90 are calendar days
human_review_trigger: No provisional credit by day 10 (or 20) with investigation still open; institution held or restricted the provisional credit
uncertainty: Low.

rule: Reasonable investigation scope
source_pinpoint: 12 CFR 1005.11(c)(4); comments 11(c)(4)-1 to -5; CFPB FAQ Error Resolution Q2, Q3; CFPB BofA order (2022)
legal_trigger: Investigation under way
obligation: Where no agreement covers the third party, review the institution's own relevant records (ACH records, account history, location of the transaction or payee relative to the consumer's residence, out-of-sequence checks, service-provider records, anything else appropriate); may not limit review to payment instructions. Network rules giving less protection do not reduce Reg E duties.
exceptions: Third party with no agreement: advising the consumer within the time period can satisfy a documentation request (comment 11(c)(4)-1)
human_review_trigger: Denial based only on device or login match, an automated fraud score, or 'the transaction was authenticated' (the CFPB found sole reliance on an automated filter unfair and a Reg E failure, S23)
uncertainty: Medium: 'reasonable' is fact-specific.

rule: No-error finding: written explanation, document access, notice before reversing provisional credit
legal_trigger: Institution determines no error (or a different error)
obligation: Written explanation of findings with notice of the right to request documents relied on; copies promptly on request. When debiting provisional credit: notify date and amount, honor checks, drafts and preauthorized transfers for 5 business days after notice without overdraft charges (only items it would have paid).
exceptions: Reassertion of the same error after full compliance creates no new duty (1005.11(e)) unless based on requested documentation
deadline: Explanation within 3 business days after investigation ends; 5 business days honoring period
clock_start: End of investigation; notice of debit
human_review_trigger: No written explanation; documents refused; provisional credit pulled without notice; overdraft fees after reversal
uncertainty: Low.

rule: Prepaid accounts: alternative timing; unverified accounts exempt
payment_rail: Prepaid cards and app balances (e.g., stored-value P2P balances)
legal_trigger: Money left a prepaid account (not payroll or government benefit)
obligation: If the provider gives online history instead of statements, the 60-day windows run from the earlier of electronic access showing the transfer or a written history; or the provider may accept notices within 120 days after posting. If the provider never verified the consumer's identity (with required disclosures), it need not apply 1005.6 or 1005.11.
exceptions: Payroll and government benefit accounts are not covered by the unverified exception
clock_start: Electronic access / written history, or posting date
human_review_trigger: Provider says the account was unverified
uncertainty: Low.

rule: Burden of proof on the institution; civil liability; treble damages; one-year limit to sue
legal_trigger: Dispute over liability; denial or procedural failure
obligation: Institution must prove the transfer was authorized, or that liability conditions were met. Consumer remedies: actual damages; statutory $100 to $1,000 (individual); class recovery capped at the lesser of $500,000 or 1% of net worth; attorney fees. Treble damages if no provisional recredit within 10 days and no good-faith investigation or no reasonable basis, or if the institution knowingly and willfully concluded no error against the evidence.
exceptions: Bona fide error defense (1693m(c))
human_review_trigger: ALWAYS route to attorney review when any R-E10, R-E11, R-E12 or R-E13 failure appears, or when the denial is near or past 9 months old
uncertainty: Low on text. How courts fix the date of the 'violation' for the 1-year limit was not researched.

rule: Remittance transfer errors (international consumer transfers through a provider)
legal_trigger: Consumer sent money abroad through a remittance provider and it arrived late, in the wrong amount, or not at all
obligation: Provider must investigate notices received within 180 days after the disclosed availability date, decide within 90 days, report within 3 business days, and remedy listed errors.
exceptions: Changes caused by sender-provided information; fraud and sanctions screening delays; being deceived about the recipient does not appear among the listed errors
clock_start: Disclosed date of availability; receipt of notice
extension_rules: Later of 180 days or 60 days after requested documentation
human_review_trigger: Scam paid via remittance service
uncertainty: Low.

rule: Credit card unauthorized use: liability capped at $50
legal_trigger: Charge made by someone without actual, implied or apparent authority, from which the cardholder got no benefit
obligation: Liability is the lesser of $50 or the value obtained before notice, and only if the card was accepted, the issuer gave notice of liability and a way to report, and provided identification means. Card obtained through fraud or robbery counts as unauthorized; card furnished to a person who exceeds authority does not, until notice.
exceptions: Authority is decided under state law (comment 12(b)(1)(ii)-1); business programs with 10 or more cards may contract otherwise, but not for employee liability
deadline: No filing deadline for the $50 cap; liability stops at notice
human_review_trigger: Issuer claims 'apparent authority' because the cardholder shared card details with a scammer
uncertainty: Medium: 'apparent authority' turns on state law.

rule: Issuer's reasonable investigation; cannot automatically deny for missing affidavit or police report
source_pinpoint: Supp. I to Part 1026, comment to 1026.12(b) on conducting a reasonable investigation (shown as 12(b)-3 on CFPB site)
legal_trigger: Issuer seeks to impose any liability
obligation: Issuer must reasonably investigate; may ask for cooperation and consider listed factors, but may not deny solely because the cardholder will not sign an affidavit or file a police report, and may not require a statement under penalty of perjury.
exceptions: If the issuer has no other information, a refusal to provide information may reasonably end the investigation
human_review_trigger: Issuer demanded a notarized or penalty-of-perjury affidavit
uncertainty: Low; confirm comment number.

rule: Billing error: written notice within 60 days; acknowledgment 30 days; resolution within 2 billing cycles and 90 days
payment_rail: Credit card and other open-end credit
legal_trigger: Statement shows an unauthorized charge, goods or services not accepted or not delivered as agreed, or another listed billing error
obligation: Written notice at the creditor's disclosed billing-error address. While unresolved: consumer need not pay the disputed amount; no adverse credit reporting or collection on it; autopay must not take it if notice arrives 3 business days before the payment date. Creditor must correct or explain after reasonable investigation.
exceptions: Phone calls do not preserve billing-error rights (written notice required); overdraft credit tied to EFTs follows Reg E instead (1026.13(i))
deadline: 60 days (notice); 30 days (acknowledgment); 2 complete billing cycles, max 90 days (resolution)
clock_start: Creditor's transmittal of the first statement with the error; receipt of notice
human_review_trigger: Caller only phoned in; creditor reported the disputed amount as late
uncertainty: Low.

rule: Claims and defenses against the card issuer for merchant disputes
legal_trigger: Consumer bought goods or services with the card and the merchant did not deliver or resolve the dispute
obligation: Consumer may withhold payment of the unpaid disputed balance and assert non-tort claims against the issuer, if they made a good-faith attempt to resolve with the merchant and the purchase exceeded $50 and was in the same state or within 100 miles of the current address.
exceptions: $50 and location limits do not apply when the merchant is the issuer or related, a franchised dealer, or the sale came from an issuer mail solicitation
deadline: None stated; limited to amount still unpaid
human_review_trigger: Online purchase scam where location of the 'merchant' is unclear
uncertainty: Medium: how the location test applies to online purchases was not researched.

rule: Card network fraud chargebacks (issuer-filed, contractual)
source_pinpoint: Visa Core Rules sec. 11.7 (Dispute Category 10, conditions 10.1-10.5); Mastercard Chargeback Guide, 4837
legal_trigger: Cardholder states they did not authorize or take part in the card transaction
obligation: Issuer may charge back to the acquirer under network fraud codes. This is the bank's tool, not a consumer right; it runs alongside Reg E or Reg Z, which control the consumer's rights.
exceptions: Transactions the cardholder took part in (scam purchases) are generally handled under non-fraud dispute codes (general industry understanding; network text not verified)
deadline: Reported by secondary sources as 120 calendar days from processing date for Visa 10.4 and Mastercard 4837
clock_start: Transaction processing date (Visa) / central processing date (Mastercard)
human_review_trigger: Bank cites a network deadline shorter than Reg E (FAQ Error Resolution Q3: network rules cannot reduce Reg E duties)
uncertainty: High on exact deadlines: primary rule text did not render (S37, S38).

rule: Consumer wires: Article 4A governs unless part of the transfer is governed by EFTA
legal_trigger: Money left by wire, including a wire ordered through online banking
obligation: Apply R-W02 to R-W05. Flag for EFTA treatment of the online consumer-to-bank leg only as a contested theory (People v. Citibank).
exceptions: Remittance transfers: 4A applies, and EFTA section 919 prevails on conflict (4A-108(b)-(c); Reg J commentary)
human_review_trigger: Every wire claim goes to specialist review
uncertainty: High while the Second Circuit appeal is pending (G-04).

rule: Unauthorized but verified payment order binds the customer if the security procedure was commercially reasonable and followed in good faith
legal_trigger: Wire sent in the customer's name that the customer did not authorize
obligation: Bank keeps the payment only if it proves an agreed, commercially reasonable security procedure, good-faith acceptance, compliance with the procedure and with any written customer restriction. Even then the customer avoids the loss by proving the order was not caused by a person entrusted with payment duties or someone who got access or security information from a source the customer controls (4A-203(a)(2)).
exceptions: Express written agreement can further limit the bank's rights; parties cannot otherwise vary these sections
human_review_trigger: All wire claims
uncertainty: Medium: commercial reasonableness is a question of law decided case by case.

rule: Refund with interest for unauthorized, unenforceable orders; 90-day reporting duty affects interest only
legal_trigger: Bank not entitled to enforce or keep payment under 4A-202/203
obligation: Bank must refund with interest from payment date to refund date. Customer who fails to use ordinary care or report within a reasonable time (max 90 days after notice of acceptance or debit) loses interest only.
exceptions: Agreement may fix the 'reasonable time'; refund duty itself cannot be varied
deadline: Reasonable time, not over 90 days (interest only)
clock_start: Customer's receipt of notice that the order was accepted or the account debited
human_review_trigger: All wire claims
uncertainty: Low on text; state enactments may differ (not checked).

rule: One-year preclusion for objecting to a wire debit
legal_trigger: Customer received notice reasonably identifying the order
obligation: Customer must object within one year of receiving the notice or is precluded from asserting the bank may not keep the payment.
exceptions: None in uniform text
clock_start: Customer's receipt of notification reasonably identifying the order
human_review_trigger: Any wire older than 9 months
uncertainty: Low on uniform text.

rule: Fedwire transfers: Reg J subpart B makes Article 4A federal law and preempts inconsistent state law
legal_trigger: Wire moved over Fedwire
obligation: Apply 4A as incorporated; subpart B prevails over Appendix A; EFTA-governed portions (other than section 919) are outside subpart B.
exceptions: Operating circulars govern operational details
human_review_trigger: All wire claims
uncertainty: Low.

rule: Checks: bank may charge only properly payable items; customer must review statements
legal_trigger: Forged or altered check paid from the account
obligation: Forged or altered items are not properly payable. Customer must review statements with reasonable promptness and report; precluded for repeat items by the same wrongdoer paid after a reasonable period not over 30 days; comparative fault if the bank lacked ordinary care; absolute bar after 1 year.
exceptions: Deposit agreements commonly shorten the reporting period by contract (examples in tab E)
human_review_trigger: All check claims (route to specialist)
uncertainty: Medium: contract periods and state variations not checked.

rule: Consumer unauthorized ACH debit returns (R05, R07, R10, R11) within 60 days with a Written Statement of Unauthorized Debit
source_pinpoint: Nacha Operating Rules (summaries): Differentiating Unauthorized Return Reasons; Risk Management Topics Oct 1, 2024
legal_trigger: A company pulled money from a consumer account without valid authorization, after authorization was revoked, or not as authorized
obligation: Bank-to-bank right of the receiving bank (RDFI) to return the debit; consumer signs a WSUD (may be signed once the entry is presented, even before posting); RDFI must return by the opening of the 6th banking day after completing review of the signed WSUD. Separately, Reg E error resolution applies to the consumer.
exceptions: Corporate accounts: R29, 2 banking days; disputes about goods or services are excluded from R10/R11
clock_start: Settlement date of the original entry
human_review_trigger: Business account; caller past 60 days from settlement (Reg E may still apply)
uncertainty: Medium: Nacha rule text is licensed; R05 and R07 descriptions from bank summaries.

rule: ACH 'false pretenses' fraud monitoring (2026) creates institution duties, not a consumer refund right
source_pinpoint: Nacha Risk Management Topics: Fraud Monitoring Phase 1 (Mar 20, 2026) and Phase 2 (June 19, practical June 22, 2026); R06 status reply in 10 banking days (Apr 1, 2025); R17 codified (Oct 1, 2024)
legal_trigger: Consumer pushed ACH credit to a scammer (e.g., impersonation)
obligation: Banks must run risk-based monitoring for entries initiated due to fraud, including 'false pretenses' (misrepresented identity, association or account ownership). The sending bank may request a return (R06); the receiving bank must respond within 10 banking days and may return suspected fraud with R17. None of this obliges reimbursement.
exceptions: 'False pretenses' excludes poor-quality or non-existent goods
human_review_trigger: None by default; useful as a recovery request in the dispute packet
uncertainty: Medium: summaries only.

rule: Zelle network: participating banks must reimburse 'qualifying imposter scams' (voluntary network policy)
source_pinpoint: EWS statement, June 30, 2023; Senate Banking letter, Feb 15, 2024
legal_trigger: Caller sent a Zelle payment to someone impersonating a bank, business or government agency
obligation: Ask the sending bank to review under the Zelle imposter-scam rule. Qualifying criteria and deadlines are not public; the bank decides.
exceptions: EWS said the policy is 'not carte blanche for all imposter scams'; purchase scams and romance scams are generally outside it (secondary reporting)
human_review_trigger: Denial with no stated reason; impersonated entity was the caller's own bank
uncertainty: High: network rules are non-public.

rule: Brokerage accounts: route to FINRA framework, not Reg E
legal_trigger: Money or securities left a brokerage or investment account
obligation: Customer disputes with a member firm or associated person arising from its business must go to FINRA arbitration if a written agreement requires it or the customer requests it. Claims are ineligible after 6 years from the event. Firms must keep written customer complaints for 4 years (useful for evidence requests).
exceptions: Insurance business of a member that is also an insurer is excluded from the business-activity condition
clock_start: Occurrence or event giving rise to the claim
human_review_trigger: Always route to securities specialist
uncertainty: Low.

rule: Call recording consent: obtain consent from everyone on the call
source_pinpoint: 18 U.S.C. 2511(2)(d) (federal one-party); Cal. Penal Code 632, 632.7; Fla. Stat. 934.03; 720 ILCS 5/14-2; Md. Cts. & Jud. Proc. 10-402; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 272 sec. 99; Mont. Code 45-8-213; N.H. RSA 570-A:2; 18 Pa.C.S. 5703-5704; RCW 9.73.030; Conn. Gen. Stat. 52-570d (civil, phone); Del. Code tit. 11 sec. 2402; Nevada by case law
legal_trigger: Recording or transcribing an intake call
obligation: Announce recording and AI transcription at the start and get affirmative consent before substantive questions; treat every call as all-party because caller location may be unknown and California applies its law to calls with a California party (Kearney v. Salomon Smith Barney, per secondary source).
exceptions: One-party states permit recording by a participant, but a product cannot rely on caller location
human_review_trigger: Caller declines recording (switch to no-record mode or human)
uncertainty: Medium: statutes cited via a secondary compendium; Connecticut, Delaware, Nevada and Oregon readings vary.

rule: AI voice disclosure and outbound-call consent
source_pinpoint: FCC Declaratory Ruling FCC 24-17 (TCPA, 47 U.S.C. 227); Utah Code 13-75 as amended by SB 226 (2025)
legal_trigger: Using an AI voice to call consumers, or a generative AI agent collecting financial data and giving personalized information
obligation: Outbound calls using an AI-generated voice need the TCPA's prior express consent. In Utah, disclose AI use on a clear request, and up front in 'high-risk' interactions (financial data plus personalized information relied on for significant decisions) for regulated occupations. Product default: disclose AI at call start.
